teaser: A duke's son begged his mother for the money to buy her. He only ever called her “the naked woman.”

lesson.text: This picture was never meant for a museum wall. It was painted for a private room in the palace of a duke's family, most likely a bedroom or the chamber next to it. Very few people were supposed to see it: the owner, his wife, a handful of guests he trusted. Keep that small room in mind. It changes everything about how she looks at you.

The buyer was Guidobaldo della Rovere, the 24-year-old heir to the Duchy of Urbino, a small state in central Italy. In 1538 he wrote to his agent in Venice, anxious that Titian might sell the canvas to someone else. In those letters he never says “Venus.” He writes simply of “the naked woman.”
Guidobaldo did not have the cash. He asked his mother, the Duchess of Urbino, to help him pay for the picture, and she was not eager. The agent was told to stay in Venice until the painting was his.

Titian, about 50, was by then the most wanted painter in Venice. For the pose he reached back almost thirty years, to a sleeping goddess in a landscape begun by his friend Giorgione, which Titian himself had finished after Giorgione died young. Then he made two changes: he woke her up, and he brought her indoors.
Indoors, Titian needs a way to organize a room around a body. Watch how he cuts the canvas into pieces.

lines.label: The dark edge
lines.text: A dark screen ends in a sharp vertical edge, right at the middle of the canvas. Follow it down: it lands on her left hand. The architecture itself points at the most charged spot in the picture.

lines.label: One long line
lines.text: Her body runs from the top left to the bottom right in a single, slow slope, from the head on the pillows to the tip of the foot. Nothing interrupts it.

lines.label: A second picture
lines.text: The right half opens like a painting inside the painting: a tiled floor, two servants, a window, evening sky. It gives the eye somewhere to breathe, and tells you whose house this is.

lesson.text: So the canvas has two halves. On the left, a closed, dark corner where a woman lies very near you. On the right, a bright household going about its day. The picture is about how the two belong together, and the details are there to tell you so.

lesson.title: Reading the clues
lesson.text: Four details, each of which a viewer in 1538 would have read like a word in a sentence.

spots.title: The gaze
spots.text: She is awake and she looks straight out, head tilted, without surprise or shame. In a small private room, the person she is looking at is the owner of the painting.

spots.title: Roses
spots.text: A loose bunch of roses slips from her right hand. Roses belonged to Venus, the goddess of love, and they are the nearest thing to a label for a goddess that the picture offers.

spots.title: The ring
spots.text: Her left hand rests between her thighs, and on its little finger sits a small dark ring. With the bracelet and the pearl earring, it is all she wears.

spots.title: The dog
spots.text: A small spaniel sleeps curled at her feet. Dogs stood for faithfulness, in marriage above all. This one is so calm that nobody entering the room can be a stranger.

lesson.text: A ring, a faithful dog, the flowers of the goddess of love. Many historians read the picture as a painting about marriage. Guidobaldo had married Giulia Varano in 1534, when she was still a child, and a picture like this may have been meant to celebrate the union and to show his young wife what was hoped of her. Others see nothing but a beautiful woman on a bed. The letters do not settle it.
The background holds one more argument for the marriage theory, and it is easy to miss because the two servants are so busy.
One of the servants has almost disappeared into a piece of furniture. Find her.

spots.title: The chest
spots.text: A girl in white kneels with her head and arms inside a large carved chest, while a woman in red waits with a dress over her shoulder. Chests like this, called cassoni, held a bride's clothes and came with her into a marriage.

lesson.text: On the windowsill above the chest stands a potted shrub clipped into a ball. It is usually identified as myrtle, an evergreen sacred to Venus and a traditional plant of weddings. Whatever you decide about the woman, the room around her is furnished with promises.
The name “Venus” was attached to the painting years later. There is no Cupid here, no shell, no sea, nothing that marks a goddess for certain. The roses and the myrtle are the only hints.

Now the paint itself. Titian worked in oil on canvas, building the skin from thin, half-transparent layers laid over one another, so that light seems to come from inside the body. Against the cool white sheets and the deep green curtain, the flesh looks warm enough to touch. Venetian painters were famous for this: color first, outline second.

The canvas left Urbino in 1631, when the last heiress of the family married a Medici and carried her inheritance to Florence. It has been one of the stars of the Uffizi ever since, and the private picture became one of the most public nudes in Europe.

Not everyone was charmed. After visiting the Uffizi, the American writer Mark Twain called it “the foulest, the vilest, the obscenest picture the world possesses” in his 1880 travel book A Tramp Abroad, partly as a joke about what art is allowed to show and books are not.

A young French painter, Édouard Manet, copied it in Florence in the 1850s. A few years later he repainted it his own way: same pose, same steady gaze, but a modern Parisian woman, and a black cat where the sleeping dog had been. His Olympia caused a scandal in 1865. The question both pictures ask is still the same one: who is she looking at, and what does she expect of you?

quiz.question: Where was this painting meant to hang?
options: In a private room of a ducal palace
quiz.explanation: It was bought by the heir of Urbino for a private chamber, seen by very few people.

quiz.question: What did Guidobaldo call the picture in his letters?
quiz.explanation: He never used the name Venus, which was attached later.

quiz.question: What is the kneeling servant doing?
options: Reaching into a chest of clothes
quiz.explanation: She leans into a cassone, a chest of the kind that held a bride's clothes.

quiz.question: Which earlier picture gave Titian the pose?
options: A sleeping goddess begun by Giorgione
quiz.explanation: Titian had finished Giorgione's sleeping nude himself, then woke her and brought her indoors.

quiz.question: What does the dark vertical edge in the middle of the canvas lead to?
quiz.explanation: The edge of the screen falls exactly on her hand.

facts.text: The little dog at her feet is wide awake and barking.
facts.explanation: The spaniel is asleep, a sign of faithfulness and of a calm household.

facts.text: Manet's Olympia replaces the dog with a black cat.
facts.explanation: Manet reworked Titian's composition and swapped the sleeping dog for a cat.

facts.text: The painting has been in Urbino ever since it was made.
facts.explanation: It went to Florence in 1631 with the family's last heiress.
